confidence_boundary: This checkpoint confirms challenger derivation and combatant ordering for the two normal collision-to-battle paths. It does not yet prove that every scripted or direct setter caller preserves standing-target-first ordering.

normal_collision_event_fields.initialization: Constructor 0x022637AC reads the active-shot object through session +0x298, loads byte +0x1E8, subtracts one, and stores the resulting descriptor index at event +0x16.
Constructor 0x022637AC initializes the field to 0xFF. Collision-target selection later replaces it with a valid standing-target descriptor index in the branches ending at 0x02264E10 or 0x02264F84.

challenging_participant_derivation: Read the active thrown descriptor index from collision event +0x16.
The normal collision caller passes that index as setter argument r2.
Setter 0x02262A64 stores r2 into session +0x28E, selecting combatant record 1.
Resolve the descriptor at session +0x7C + descriptor_index * 20.
Extract the low nibble of descriptor byte +0x0F as the challenging participant index.

runtime_control.displayed_state: Shuji's participant-1 Bakugan was already standing on the active Gate, and participant 0 was instructed to throw onto the same Gate to start the battle.
runtime_control.interpretation: The exact runtime record mapping matches the normal collision call order: participant 1 is the standing target in record 0, while participant 0 is the incoming challenger in record 1.

supported_conclusions: For normal collision-triggered battles, combatant record 0 is standing-target-first and combatant record 1 is incoming-challenger-second.
The canonical normal-path challenging participant is not the value stored directly at session +0x28E. It is the low nibble of byte +0x0F in the descriptor selected by session +0x28E.
Gate ownership and challenger identity are independent. Gate owner remains battle object +0x06, while challenger comes from the active thrown descriptor.
Both normal collision-to-battle call sites use the same standing-target-first argument order.
System 2.0 may derive normal-path self/opponent relationships from participant indices, but must not treat record index alone as a universal owner or human/AI identity.
